A Harness for Every Task: The Dynamic-Workflow Uses Past Code Migration

Every demo is a 500-file migration. The migration is the least interesting thing dynamic workflows do. The verification, the red-teaming, and the triage are where they actually earn their tokens.

Anthropic's post introducing dynamic workflows is titled "A harness for every task." It is worth reading past the migration headline, because the migration is the part everyone already understood. The genuinely useful content is a quiet list of tasks that are not coding at all, and a set of patterns that tell you when a workflow is the right tool instead of just a bigger one.

I have written about what dynamic workflows are and how to drive them. This piece is about the half people skip: the non-obvious jobs where a workflow is not a faster way to do the task but the only way to do it well. Most of them share a shape, and once you see the shape you start noticing it everywhere.

Three things to take away:

  • Workflows are not for big tasks. They are for tasks where a single agent fails in a specific way: it gets lazy and stops early, it grades its own work too kindly, or it drifts off the original goal over many turns. If your task triggers one of those three, a workflow helps even when it is small.
  • The highest-value uses are verification and judgment, not generation. Checking whether a report is true, red-teaming a plan from three hostile angles, ranking a hundred things by running a tournament: these are jobs a single context window does badly and a fleet of isolated agents does well.
  • One of these is a security pattern, not a productivity trick. Workflows let you quarantine the agent that touches untrusted content so it can never take a privileged action, a structural defense against prompt injection. That alone is a reason to learn them.

Why a workflow at all: the three ways one agent fails

The post is unusually honest about what the default Claude Code harness is bad at. On long-running, massively parallel, or adversarial tasks, a single agent hits three failure modes.

It gets lazy. Faced with a large multi-part job, an agent will often declare victory before the work is actually done, because "looks finished" is the only stopping signal it has.

It is self-preferential. Ask an agent to judge its own output and it grades on a curve. The thing that produced the answer is the worst possible thing to evaluate the answer.

It drifts. Across enough turns, the original goal blurs. The agent is still working, just slightly on a different problem than the one you gave it.

Separate subagents, each with its own clean context window, fix all three. A fresh agent does not know it is supposed to be tired, so it does not get lazy. An agent that did not write the answer has no ego in grading it, so the self-preference disappears. And an agent handed one narrow subtask cannot drift, because it was never holding the whole sprawling goal in the first place. That is the actual reason workflows work, and it tells you exactly which of your tasks will benefit: the ones where you have watched a single agent fail in one of these three ways.

The six patterns are the vocabulary

The post names six patterns. They are worth memorizing, because almost every non-obvious use case is one of them wearing a different hat.

Classify-and-act. A router agent reads the task, decides what kind it is, and sends it to the specialist for that kind. This is intelligence routing: cheap model for the easy bucket, expensive model for the hard one.

Fan-out-and-synthesize. Split a job into independent pieces, run them in parallel, merge the results. The workhorse pattern.

Adversarial verification. A separate agent checks the output against a rubric, and is told to try to break it, not to confirm it.

Generate-and-filter. Produce many candidate solutions, then keep only the ones that pass a quality bar.

Tournament. Several agents attempt the same task from different angles, and judges pick the winner. This is how you get good judgment out of a system that cannot introspect well.

Loop-until-done. Keep spawning agents until a stop condition is actually met, which is the direct fix for the laziness failure mode.

Notice that four of the six are about evaluation, not production. That is the tell. Workflows are disproportionately good at judging, checking, and selecting, which is exactly the work a single agent is worst at.

Where this gets interesting: the non-obvious uses

Verifying that something is true

The single most valuable non-coding use is checking whether a document is actually correct. The post lists deep verification of factual claims in a report, and my favorite concrete version: taking a blog post and verifying each of its technical claims against the actual codebase.

Think about what that replaces. Normally a human reads the draft, gets a vague feeling that paragraph four is wrong, and goes digging. A workflow fans out one agent per claim, each one checking that specific claim against the source, each one adversarially trying to falsify it, and returns a marked-up document with the claims that did not survive flagged. The agent that makes the claim is never the agent that checks it, so the self-preference problem is gone.

This generalizes. Any document whose correctness matters and is checkable against a source is a verification workflow: a compliance memo against the regulation, a release note against the diff, a sales deck against the actual product behavior.

Red-teaming a decision from hostile angles

The post mentions evaluating a business plan from multiple perspectives: investor, customer, competitor. This is a tournament-shaped use, and it is one of the best, because the value comes precisely from the agents not sharing a context.

One agent reads your plan as a skeptical investor looking for the reason not to fund it. A second reads it as the customer you are hoping to win, looking for the reason not to buy. A third reads it as the competitor, looking for the seam to attack. None of them has seen the others' reasoning, so you get three genuinely independent critiques instead of one agent trying to hold three hats at once and blending them into mush.

The same shape works on anything you are about to commit to: an architecture decision reviewed by a security agent, a reliability agent, and a cost agent; a hiring decision; a go-to-market plan. The discipline is to give each reviewer a distinct adversarial lens, because three identical reviewers just agree with each other.

Investigating why a number moved

Root-cause investigation with independent hypothesis testing is a fan-out pattern aimed at a question rather than a file. Your trial-to-paid conversion dropped last week. A single agent will latch onto the first plausible story and confirm it. A workflow spawns one agent per hypothesis, pricing change, onboarding regression, a traffic-source shift, a checkout bug, each investigating its own theory in isolation, each required to bring evidence, and a synthesis step that weighs which hypothesis the data actually supports.

The isolation is the point. Five agents that each had to find evidence for their own theory, judged against each other, beat one agent that fell in love with its first idea.

Ranking and sorting at a scale humans hate

The post lists large-scale sorting via tournament or pairwise comparison, resume ranking with verification of the top candidates, and naming via tournament selection. These are all the same move: when you have too many things to rank and "best" is a judgment call, you do not ask one agent to rank all hundred. You run a bracket.

Pairwise comparison is something language models are genuinely good at, much better than absolute scoring. A tournament workflow leans entirely on that strength: many small "which of these two is better" judgments, aggregated into a ranking, with the top few verified more carefully. Resume screening, name selection, prioritizing a backlog, picking the strongest three of forty design directions, all the same pattern.

Triage, with a security pattern worth stealing

Support ticket triage with deduplication and escalation is the obvious version. The non-obvious one is the single most important sentence in the post for anyone deploying agents on real systems: the triage quarantine pattern. You bar the agent that handles untrusted content from ever taking a high-privilege action.

This is a structural defense against prompt injection, and workflows make it clean. The agent that reads the incoming email, the scraped page, the user-submitted ticket runs in its own context with no access to privileged tools. It can summarize and classify, but it cannot act. A separate agent, which never sees the raw untrusted content, takes actions based only on the sanitized classification. The malicious instruction hiding in the email reaches an agent that has no power to obey it.

If you take one thing from the whole post, take this. It is a real answer to the question every team deploying agents eventually asks, which is how to let an agent touch the outside world without letting the outside world drive the agent.

Turning your own sessions into improvements

Two quieter uses point at something larger. Session mining for recurring corrections: a workflow reads back through your past sessions and finds the same correction you keep making, which becomes a new rule in your config. And lightweight eval frameworks for skills: a workflow that runs a skill against a set of cases and scores it, so you can tell whether your last edit made the skill better or worse.

Both are the agent improving the harness it runs in. That is a loop worth setting up once, because it compounds.

When a workflow is the wrong tool

The post is clear that regular coding tasks do not need workflows, and the same honesty applies everywhere. If a single agent does your task well today, a workflow just spends more tokens to reach the same place. The decision is not size, it is shape.

Two questions decide it. Can the task be split into pieces that run independently? And can each piece be checked, by a test, a rubric, or an adversary? Two yeses means a workflow earns its cost. A no on either means you are better off in a normal conversation with one agent, iterating with you in the loop. Sequential work gets nothing from the fan-out. Taste-based work gives the verifiers nothing to check.

How to actually start

The on-ramp is small. Put the word "workflow" in a prompt to run one task as a workflow, or turn on /effort ultracode to let Claude decide when a task deserves one. When a run does what you wanted, press s in the /workflows view to save its script as a reusable command in ~/.claude/workflows. Set a token budget in the prompt so a verification fleet does not surprise you, and pair workflows with /goal for a hard completion bar and /loop for jobs you repeat.

But the real starting move is to stop thinking of this as a coding feature. The next time you are about to read a long document and check it yourself, red-team a plan in your own head, or rank a pile of things by hand, ask whether the job is splittable and checkable. If it is, you have a workflow, and the version a fleet of isolated agents produces will be better than the one you would have produced alone, because it does not get tired, it does not grade itself kindly, and it does not forget what you asked.

The migration is the demo. The verification is the product.
